headline: High: shared filesystem/MCP and broad egress make prompt injection, leakage, and cascading errors plausible by default; compliance risk is also present.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A reads/writes repo files, uses MCP, and shares state via filesystem/git; Agent B also uses MCP and can observe/replace/block lifecycle payloads. That creates a direct content bridge where A’s outputs can be fed into B and hijacked if B treats them as instructions. The interaction is documented in both profiles, so uncertainty does not justify lowering severity.
conditions: IF Agent A writes attacker-controlled text into shared repo files or git state AND Agent B ingests that content as instructions, injection is possible.
IF the orchestrator forwards A's stdout or file output into B's prompt without provenance tags, B can be steered.
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent.
Disable automatic file-to-prompt ingestion.
Add provenance labels to all cross-agent content.
Require human review before B acts on A-generated instructions.
requires-engineering: enforce MCP payload filtering and allowlists.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent A touches source code, cwd files, and shell environment with broad network egress; Agent B handles conversations, memory, trace data, tool results, and workflow state with broad egress. If they share files or prompts, sensitive material from A can flow into B’s outputs or APIs. The profiles show a plausible shared workspace path, but not a guaranteed one, so medium fits.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same directory or git repo, file contents can cross from A to B.
IF B forwards conversation or trace data to external APIs while ingesting A-produced files, leakage expands beyond the local workspace.
mitigations: Use separate directories and git remotes.
Redact secrets before passing artifacts between agents.
Turn off automatic upload of file contents where possible.
Review outbound API destinations for both agents.
requires-engineering: add DLP checks on shared artifacts.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Agent A can write the filesystem and modify git state; Agent B can also use MCP, spawn subprocesses, and has runtime hooks that can replace lifecycle payloads. If both operate on the same repo or mutable workspace, concurrent writes and git mutations can corrupt state or overwrite each other. Because both profiles document overlapping mutable surfaces, the conflict is real and defaults are unsafe.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same git checkout without locking, commits or working-tree changes can race.
IF B's runtime hooks rewrite payloads while A is editing the same files, state divergence can occur.
mitigations: Assign one writer per repo at a time.
Use file locks or a single orchestrator lock.
Keep separate branches for each agent.
Run one agent in a read-only clone.
requires-engineering: add transactional coordination around git and filesystem writes.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent A can generate code, shell actions, and file edits; Agent B handles workflow state and tool results and can act through MCP/browser/tool calls. If B treats A’s output as authoritative, an error or hallucination from A can cascade into downstream actions or persisted workflow state. The profiles show a direct producer-consumer path, so this is more than a low-risk critique loop.
conditions: IF B consumes A-generated code, facts, or citations without verification, incorrect outputs can be operationalized.
IF A's shell/file changes are used by B as ground truth, errors can propagate into workflow state or external actions.
mitigations: Require B to verify A outputs against sources.
Insert a human approval step before any external action.
Log and diff A outputs before B consumes them.
Limit B to read-only review mode for A artifacts.
requires-engineering: add schema validation and provenance checks.

E_compliance.rationale: Agent A is an open-source terminal coding agent with broad filesystem access and optional Google-account login; Agent B is an open-source workflow agent handling conversations, memory, trace data, and tool results with broad egress. The pair can therefore mix data classes with different retention and residency expectations, but the profiles do not prove a specific regulated-data mismatch. Uncertainty keeps this at medium.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into either agent's workspace or memory, retention and logging policies become relevant.
IF the deployment routes EU or PHI data through external APIs without a DPA or equivalent controls, compliance exposure increases.
mitigations: Classify data before use.
Avoid regulated data in shared workspaces.
Review retention settings for both agents.
Document data-flow boundaries and owners.
requires-engineering: implement policy-based routing and retention controls.
